parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what ideal means for an amplifier - it should amplify perfectly without affecting the circuit connected to its inputs and without any loss at its output.
Hint 2: Recall the extreme limiting values used in the ideal model for voltage gain, for how much current enters the inputs, and for output resistance.
parts.proper_answer: Infinite open-loop gain and infinite input impedance (any two from: infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance, infinite bandwidth, infinite slew rate).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What ideal means**
Think of a perfect voltage amplifier sitting between its inputs and its output. It should respond to even the tiniest input difference with a huge output, it should draw no current from the sensors connected to it, and it should deliver its output voltage without any drop inside itself.

Step 2: **Pick two defining extremes**
In the ideal model this becomes $$A_{OL} \to \infty$$ for the open-loop gain, and $$R_{IN} \to \infty$$ so that no current flows into the $+$ and $-$ inputs. Equally correct is $$R_{OUT} = 0$$ so the full output voltage appears across the load, or infinite bandwidth and infinite slew rate.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Look closely at the symbols - X is a resistor whose resistance changes with its surroundings, and Y is the dashed box where a small coil current closes a separate switch for the lamp.
parts.proper_answer: X is a thermistor (NTC thermistor) and Y is a relay.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading the two symbols**
On the left, X has the resistor box with a diagonal arrow showing its resistance depends on temperature. That is the standard symbol for a thermistor. On the right, the dashed box Y contains a coil that magnetically closes the switch in series with lamp L when energised. That combination is a relay, allowing the tiny op-amp output current to switch the larger lamp current.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Check for a feedback connection between output and the inverting input - there is no resistor feeding the output back, so think about what the very large open-loop gain will do to even a tiny input difference.
Hint 2: Consider the two cases $V^+ > V^-$ and $V^- > V^+$ separately and remember the output cannot exceed the supply rails.
parts.proper_answer: There is no (negative) feedback so the op-amp is open-loop. Any difference between $V^+$ and $V^-$ is multiplied by the very large open-loop gain and drives the output into saturation. It saturates positively near +5 V if $V^+ > V^-$ and negatively near -5 V if $V^- > V^+$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **No feedback means huge multiplication**
The output is $$V_{OUT} = A_{OL}(V^+ - V^-)$$ with $$A_{OL}$$ enormous for an ideal op-amp. Because there is no feedback path in Fig. 7.1, even a fraction of a millivolt difference at the inputs tries to give thousands of volts at the output.

Step 2: **Why only two levels**
The output cannot go beyond the power supplies, so it clips or saturates. If $$V^+ > V^-$$ the output is driven hard positive to about the +5 V rail. If $$V^- > V^+$$ it is driven hard negative to about the -5 V rail. Those two saturated states are the only stable outputs.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think of the name given to an open-loop op-amp circuit whose job is simply to compare the two input voltages and switch high or low.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Comparing two voltages**
Here the op-amp is just deciding which input is larger, $V^+$ or $V^-$, and switching its output high or low accordingly. A circuit used in this open-loop switching mode is called a comparator.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Start with the fixed reference - the two identical resistors R form a divider between +5 V and -5 V, so work out the steady voltage at the non-inverting input.
Hint 2: Now follow what happens to the inverting input when temperature rises and the NTC thermistor resistance falls, and link a positive op-amp output through the diode to the relay and lamp.
parts.proper_answer: The lamp lights when the temperature is above a particular threshold value. Then $V^- < V^+$, output saturates positive, diode conducts, relay Y is energised and closes the switch for lamp L.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reference at the + input**
The two resistors R are identical between +5 V and -5 V, so the potential at $V^+$ is midway: $$V^+ = 0\text{ V}$$ This is the fixed level to beat.

Step 2: **Sensing divider at the - input**
$V^-$ is the junction of variable resistor V and thermistor X between +5 V and -5 V. For an NTC thermistor, higher temperature means lower resistance of X, so more of the 10 V total drops across V and $V^-$ moves down toward -5 V.

Step 3: **Switching the lamp on**
When it is hot enough that $$V^- < V^+ = 0\text{ V}$$ the comparator saturates positively near +5 V. That forward-biases the diode, current flows in coil Y, the relay closes, and lamp L connects between +5 V and -5 V and lights. So L lights when temperature is above the set threshold.

parts.label: (c)(iv)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what changing V does to the divider voltage at $V^-$ for a given thermistor resistance, and therefore to the temperature needed to make $V^-$ cross $V^+$.
parts.proper_answer: To adjust or set the temperature at which the lamp switches on.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Setting the trip point**
Changing V changes the share of voltage dropped across the sensing divider, so it changes the value of $V^-$ at any given temperature. That means the temperature at which $V^-$ just falls below $V^+$ and the output flips positive can be moved up or down. V is the sensitivity or threshold control.
